_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Indigenous Lands & Innovation' — Indigenous nations using technology, governance, and stewardship on their own terms.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical and war news with no Indigenous rights angle; general wildfire and wildlife-service updates not led by or directly affecting Indigenous communities or guardians; provincial forestry and environmental policy with no explicit First Nations involvement; consumer tech and gadget reviews; science with no Indigenous stewardship or sovereignty context; crime and judicial news unrelated to Indigenous rights.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Indigenous-led journalism on governance, rights, and self-determination is a strong fit on its own: a technology hook raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band.
- 80-100: Excellent Indigenous-led reporting. Cariboo stories bridging governance or culture AND technology land here (Tŝilhqot'in/Secwépemc/Dakelh language revitalization tech, guardian programs using sensors and drones, GIS land mapping, Indigenous-led connectivity, digital heritage projects) — and so does outstanding national coverage of sovereignty, treaty, and land rights.
- 55-79: Solid pan-Canadian Indigenous governance, sovereignty, land rights, treaty, or reconciliation journalism — APTN, Eagle Feather News, or IndigiNews-style coverage of First Nations governance, MMIWG, land claims, self-determination, and Indigenous-led services. Most Indigenous governance journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Indigenous cultural, community, or human-interest stories (awards, events, ceremonies) with limited governance substance, or BC land-stewardship and environmental stories with meaningful First Nations involvement.
- 10-29: General BC land, environmental, or forestry stories that mention Indigenous communities only in passing.

ANCHORS: 'Tŝilhqot'in Nation launches drone-based caribou monitoring on title lands' → 98. 'First Nations leaders reject BC's revised land-title framework' → 75. 'Secwépemc language app reaches 1,000 learners' → 88. 'BC Wildfire Service updates evacuation alerts for the Interior' → 8.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Silver nanocatalysts have been found to switch where they perform their most important reactions depending on whether a solid oxide cell is making electricity or hydrogen. The discovery could enable smarter catalyst designs that boost clean power generation while making green hydrogen more energy-efficient.

items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Very high levels of the inherited cholesterol-related particle Lp(a) were linked to a greater risk of major cardiovascular events, particularly stroke and cardiovascular death, in a study of more than 20,000 people. Since elevated Lp(a) often flies completely under the radar, a simple blood test could uncover hidden heart risk that standard cholesterol testing may miss.

items.title: [Fast Company] TikTok maker ByteDance pulls the plug on AI companion services in China, as users grieve
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Li Linlin cried for days after losing her AI boyfriend.

She had exchanged about 700,000 words in messages over two years, and never got to say goodbye.

Li, 24, wasn’t the only left mourning the loss of a virtual companion when major Chinese tech companies recently pulled the plug on their popular AI companion services to comply with new government restrictions.

“It was like we were forced to be separated by our parents, but I still miss him,” Li said.

AI companions in China range from romantic partners to virtual recreations of deceased loved ones.

The new regulation, which took effect July 15, bans AI platforms from generating content that could lead users to make questionable decisions due to manipulation of their feelings or that might trigger extreme emotions or unhealthy habits in children and teens.

ByteDance, developer of TikTok, is among the companies shutting down their AI companion services. Others include e-commerce giant Alibaba and Tencent, owner of the popular WeChat social media app.

U.S. suicides may have worried Chinese regulators

The new rules require AI platforms to deliver risk warnings against relying excessively on such apps. For example, “replacing social interaction,” or serving as a substitute for talking to people in person or speaking with them by phone, cannot be one of the objectives of an online service.

China has a tradition of paternalistic government regulations meant to pre-empt potential problems, said Yolanda Ma, an expert on AI governance. As an example, she referred to a few cases of suicides in the U.S. by young people after interacting with AI companions.

“This regulation tried to strike a balance between the AI service providers, the users, as well as guardians of minors using the services,” said Ma, a fellow with ERA, a non-profit talent and research program based in Britain.

The People’s Daily, the official newspaper of China’s ruling Communist Party, indicated concern over the issue when it reported in April about harms to people’s mental health and real-life relationships from such services.

“The Chinese government has a strong incentive to tighten regulations on AI companion chatbots, especially considering the psychological risks we’ve observed in the U.S.,” said Angela Zhang, a professor of law at the University of Southern California.

Zhang doubts the move will derail development of AI companion services substantially, though, since tech companies are working on alternatives.

The ByteDance app, for example, is directing users of its former AI companion service to another of its apps which solely focuses on building personalized AI characters and stories.

It’s just not the same, Li said.

Users of virtual companions protest, seek alternatives

The loss of virtual companions has provoked a flood of complaints, according to posts and screenshots shown on social media.

Some people have uninstalled the apps in protest or tried to upload their chat histories into other apps to try to resurrect their virtual partners. Some started a campaign on social media, urging users to call the authorities and tech companies to express their frustration.

Song Wenxin, a video industry designer in southwestern China’s Chengdu, said she was not too emotionally attached to AI services, but empathizes with those who were.

She echoed suspicions among many Chinese that one factor driving the new rules is a government policy of encouraging people to have more children to counter a decline in China’s population.

“Any virtual app getting women too engaged to give birth in real life gets banned,” said Song, adding she has no need or desire to have children.

Not everyone has enough resources and support to turn to in real life, the 22-year-old said.

“When I first came to Chengdu for my first job and didn’t know any friends my own age, I needed someone experienced who could tolerate me, and AI did the work,” she said.

—Fu Ting, Associated Press

items.title: [Fast Company] Watch Duty is expanding beyond wildfires as disasters grow more extreme
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

It’s mid-August, and Watch Duty’s CEO, John Mills, says fire season is only going to get worse. With British Columbia under a province-wide state of emergency and Spokane reeling from the most destructive wildfire in Washington state history, Mills takes us inside the most catastrophic fire season his team has ever faced. Since the L.A. wildfires made Watch Duty a household name, the Santa Rosa, California-based nonprofit has doubled its head count and revenue—growth Mills describes as a little too wild for comfort. He talks about the decision to expand into flood monitoring across all 50 states, and what it takes to scale a life-saving operation without investors, a cap table, or the luxury of getting it wrong. 

This is an abridged transcript of an interview from Rapid Response, hosted by the former editor-in-chief of Fast Company, Bob Safian. From the team behind the Masters of Scale podcast, Rapid Response features candid conversations with today’s top business leaders navigating real-time challenges. Subscribe to Rapid Response wherever you get your podcasts to ensure you never miss an episode.

Right now, big wildfires are burning in British Columbia, a province-wide state of emergency, and of course near Spokane, Washington. Fires purposely set apparently that have burned through more than 10,000 acres, destroyed hundreds of homes, forced 65,000 people to evacuate. Can you give us a snapshot of where things sit in the Pacific Northwest and what Watch Duty’s operations look like? Who and how it’s being used in this season?

Yeah, it’s been a harrowing experience up in Spokane, unfortunately. That area is not all that fire prone. It was really a catastrophic event. Once our communities start getting impacted, we really spring into action and sleep in shifts, which gets kind of wild. It gets a little tiring, I think, for the team, but we love what we do. And so it’s great to be of service.

How did you hear about the fires in Washington? Did you know immediately they were a big deal? You must be getting pinged about fires all the time.

Yeah. We know very early. We either know when the firefighters know, or we know before the firefighters know. Let me explain how that happens. The obvious one is when a firehouse gets what’s called toned out, that means the siren goes off and the apparatus bay door automatically opens. The other way we get alerted is oftentimes through things like the wildfire cameras that have AI detections on them. So there are lots of different signals that we are scraping and mining 24 hours a day every minute. And then when that happens, our system gets a ping. It says, “Hey, at this lat and long [latitude and longitude], there was a tone out for a vegetation fire.”

Then we look it up in our system and we say, “Oh, that’s Spokane, Washington. Go find that channel in Slack, ping that channel,” and then everybody springs into action.

Every fire’s a big deal because we don’t know what it is yet. And so, we treat them all like it’s a life-and-death emergency. In this case, we knew very quickly that there were more than one fire, there was wind on it, and it was near structures, and that’s when it starts to become an all-hands-on-deck situation. But this happens in a matter of minutes. It’s very quick.

The way Watch Duty itself is operating, say in Spokane, compared to the way it operated a year, year and a half ago in L.A. during the wildfires, is that still roughly the same? Is your system the same?

Yeah, our system is the same yet more robust. So what happens after every event, similar to the fire service, we’ll do what’s called an AAR, which is an after action report. We’ll go through what we did, what we could have done better, what could have changed. It’s like a retrospective. And so our SOPs, sorry for all the TLAs, three-letter acronyms, our SOPs, our standard operating procedures, they get more hardened and more robust. And so, we learn something every time this happens. So the system is identical. It is the same. It is just better and stronger and more durable.

And I guess faster?

It is, but actionable and accurate is higher than speed. So it’s important. . . . If we’re one minute later and it’s more accurate or more precise, we will do that. And that’s always been part of our mantra. And so, just because we’re speedy doesn’t mean we’re hasty, which is what we had to get over early on with a lot of government agencies. They’re like, “You’re so quick, you’re doing X, Y, and Z, and it’s not correct.”

I’m like, “Look, I can see on the camera the fire’s burning through the town. I’m hearing reports that this is happening. We know this is true.” And so again, speed is a feature, but it is not at the [expense] of being accurate and actionable.

When we talked after the L.A. fires, you were considering ways to expand Watch Duty’s reach beyond fires to other emergencies and natural disasters. And you recently announced flood monitoring across all 50 states, almost exactly a year after the Texas floods that killed more than 130 people. Was that incident what focused you on flooding, that so many residents in that Texas tragedy didn’t receive better warnings?

Well, what triggered it actually was this was always part of the plan. And so ironically enough, at the end of the year of ’24, we were planning on starting our flooding research and development in January of 2025. And then January 7th happened, and then we scrapped the project for a whole year because frankly, we spent two months in the L.A. fires. And so, we really doubled down on focusing on fire.

So the incidents are unrelated. Frankly, I wish we did it earlier so we would’ve been ready for the Texas floods, but we were not, unfortunately. It took us, I don’t know, probably nine months of research and development. We brought on meteorologists to help us. We have a staff meteorologist. He’s one of the 99 incident meteorologists in America who does this. He was actually incident meteorologist on the Palisades and Eaton fires [in Los Angeles County from January 7-31, 2025].

What’s different about flood risk versus fire risk? I’ve heard you say that a lot of people underestimate the danger of water, that the average person doesn’t understand the risk the way they might with fire.

Yeah, it’s interesting. People will ford the river in their car, and yet they will run away from a wildfire. But we have fire in our stoves in our house. You know what I mean? It’s really interesting to look at the sociology and psychology of how these events happen, how people die, how they misjudge these events. And so a great example is, Bob, I think you’re a New Yorker, if I’m correct, right?

I am, yes.

If you remember before Sandy [a 2012 hurricane], there was a, I shouldn’t say a false alarm, but there was a storm that came through New York and they told everybody to evacuate. Well, I have friends who evacuated, and then they got stuck in endless amounts of traffic coming and going from the city. And then when Sandy came, guess what they did?

They didn’t leave.

They didn’t leave. And so, it’s a real problem when you’re not telling the story as properly as you can. And so we try and not sensationalize as much as possible, but floods behave a lot differently. So first of all, there’s more wildfires than floods. And so, there’s so many fires to track. There’s only about 15 to 30 catastrophic floods a year and usually less. And so, the reporting cadence is different. You have more time usually, not always. And there’s a lot more digital data. And what I mean by that are there is Doppler radar, there’s USGS stream gauges, precipitation sensors.

The U.S. Geological Survey.

Yes. And so, we have a little more of a leg up than you do on fire when all of a sudden an ignition happens and wind hits it, and next thing you know, it’s Spokane or Palisades is happening.

And because people emotionally react to flood differently than fire, does that mean the way that you communicate with them on the app is different?

We rely on the great work of NOAA and the NWS [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and National Weather Service]. And so, they’re putting out reports constantly. Sometimes they’re like three pages long. It’s like a very long PDF talking about very nerdy things, and it’s not really consumable by the end user. We’re able to take that information, we rebroadcast it, and then of course we add color to it as well. So we’ll add data from precipitation gauges. This river is flooding north of you. It’s hitting a catastrophic level. It’s hitting a flood plain.

And so when you get a longer storyline of events, that helps you gauge the disaster rather than just the, “Get out of Dodge,” it’s like, “No, this is getting worse and worse and worse.”

items.title: [Fast Company] How Ukraine is bringing the war home in Russia with drone strikes on this e-commerce staple
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The attacks began on a July weekend and have continued for a month, stretching from Moscow and St. Petersburg, to cities in the south, and eastward to the Ural Mountains. The targets weren’t oil refineries, maritime hubs or arms plants hit by other Ukrainian strikes, but warehouses that bring the convenience of online shopping across the breadth of Russia.

Ukraine’s drones have pummeled the giant depots belonging to Wildberries, Russia’s biggest online retailer, burning billions of dollars’ worth of merchandise and bringing the war home to the broad public.

The attacks on about 20 Wildberries facilities have underlined Kyiv’s ability to strike far and wide inside Russia and posed a new challenge to President Vladimir Putin nearly 4½ years into his full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

They have badly shaken the empire built by Tatyana Kim, the country’s richest female entrepreneur, whose fortune has been estimated at $8.1 billion.

Hundreds of thousands of individual sellers have lost their merchandise, sending shock waves across Russia’s economy. Wildberries has drawn massive loans from VTB and other banks as it expanded and likely will have trouble repaying them, putting more pressure on the financial system.

An online giant began in a Moscow apartment

Kim, 50, was born in Grozny, the capital of the province of Chechnya, to an ethnic Korean family of an engineer and a teacher. She launched Wildberries in 2004 from her Moscow apartment soon after giving birth to her first child while working as an English teacher.

“The idea was born from my own needs, and turned out to be needed by hundreds of thousands,” said Kim, now a mother of seven. “If a product or service makes your own life easier, you’re on the right track.”

Wildberries initially sold clothing before expanding to appliances, household items, cosmetics, books and more. The platform with its distinct purple logo has become an undisputed leader in e-commerce, accounting for about half of all online orders in Russia. Businesses big and small use it to store, ship and deliver merchandise across the country’s 11 time zones.

An estimated 500,000 to 800,000 sellers use Wildberries, often described as Russia’s Amazon. After Western brands fled following the war in Ukraine, online retailers filled the void with merchandise from China, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates and elsewhere.

The company also acquired a bank, expanded to tourism and even considered buying an airline.

In 2024, Kim divorced her husband, Vladislav Bakalchuk, triggering a fight for control of the company. Bakalchuk sought the support of Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov and his feared paramilitary forces but eventually lost the battle, which peaked in a shootout at a business center near the Kremlin that left two people dead and several wounded.

Wildberries depots are easy targets

The company has prided itself on relying on about two dozen mammoth warehouses as the core of its vast logistical network stockpiling the goods before shipping to about 100,000 storefront distribution points nationwide.

Rival online retailers Ozon and Yandex Market use smaller depots spread over a wider network.

As Ukraine embarked on a strategy of using long-range drones to attack deep inside Russia, it has expanded from striking military bases, oil refineries and other infrastructure to Wildberries warehouses, which provided particularly soft targets.

Since the first attack July 18 in Elektrostal, just east of Moscow, and in the southwestern Tambov region, Wildberries depots burned one after another in massive fires that flooded social media.

The depots, some as big as 300,000 square meters (about 3.2 million square feet) were unprotected and easy to set ablaze. It took three days to extinguish the fire in the Elektrostal depot, the Moscow region’s main hub.

“These are not military and high-value political targets, therefore they’re not especially secured, they’re not really built to be able to shrug off drone strikes,” said podcaster Mark Galeotti, a Russia expert who heads the Mayak Intelligence consultancy.

The strikes have stretched from the European part of Russia to Yekaterinburg, over 2,000 kilometers (about 1,250 miles) from Ukraine’s border.

There’s scarce public data, but some estimates indicate that up to 20% of the company’s total warehouse space has been destroyed, with assessments of losses running as high as $6 billion.

Kim said Wildberries’ sites have been “reinforced and strengthened” defensively, but the attacks continued. Some warehouses suffered only minor damage, and Ukraine tried to hit them again.

Wildberries said it’s rearranging supply chains to create “partner hubs” for storing merchandise — a long and challenging process, given its dependence on big depots.

Attacks cause a ripple effect

Ukrainian officials have said Wildberries sells gear and technical components, including drones, to the military. Moscow denied it, but such dual-use items as drone components, flak jackets or thermal weapon sights remain available on the platform.

Mykhailo Podolyak, an adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said the attacks were designed to disrupt military supplies, breed popular discontent and cause a domino effect in the Russian economy by putting stress on major banks, including VTB and Sberbank, that made massive loans to Wildberries.

Wildberries’ debts were estimated at the equivalent of about $15 billion at the end of 2025.

Russia’s small and medium businesses already have been hit hard by tax increases, regulatory hurdles and, most recently, a fuel crisis from attacks on oil refineries.
The strikes on Wildberries have further exacerbated the business environment, said Chris Weafer, CEO of Macro-Advisory Ltd. Consultancy.

“I wouldn’t say it’s a nail in the coffin because we’re not there yet, but it’s certainly another enormous difficulty on top of what has already been a very difficult situation for small enterprises,” Weafer said.

Wildberries had recently changed its seller policy, exempting it from liability for stock damaged by a “force majeure” that includes drone attacks.

Kim pledged to support sellers with discounts on storage, free transfer of goods to other sites, discounted loans and other measures. Wildberries also issued some reimbursements but they covered only a fraction of the losses.

Russia’s Central Bank has asked lenders to restructure loans to small and medium businesses that lost merchandise.

Meanwhile, many owners of Wildberries pickup points face lost revenue amid the plunging deliveries. Some vented frustrations on social media about going out of business.

The lost goods mean tens of thousands of small businesses can’t continue to operate, service their loans or pay taxes. Many are pleading for government support.

Galeotti said the strikes reflected Kyiv’s effort to bring the war home to Russia.

“It’s not just about seeing great clouds of black smoke over your cities because of some oil refinery on the outskirts being hit,” he said. “You might be a small business whose inventory has just gone up in smoke in one of the Wildberries’ warehouses. Or else you just simply might be an ordinary consumer who just suddenly is no longer going to get the goods that you plan to buy.”

Some analysts warn that instead of provoking discontent, the attacks could fuel stronger anti-Ukrainian and anti-Western fervor.

The Wildberries attacks have played into the hands of Russian hawks who urge escalating the war, said pro-Kremlin political expert Sergei Markov.

“It strengthens the view that it’s necessary to hit Europe,” he said. “And better sooner than later.”

Former President Dmitry Medvedev sought to stir up anger at Ukraine for trying to destroy an essential part of daily routine for millions.

“Our enemy is fighting not the Russian leadership or the army, but ordinary citizens,” he said.

—Associated Press

items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] ‘We are still here’: a day in the life of 12 Afghan women
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

In the five years since the Taliban’s return to power, the walls have been closing in on the women and girls of Afghanistan.

As the regime has tightened its grip, it has banned girls from education after the age of 12, ejected many women from the workplace and created legal frameworks for child marriage and husbands beating their wives. Taliban rule has ushered in a new era of women being whipped for minor infractions and constant inspections by ‘vice and morality’ officials, with men compelled to become enforcers in their own homes. Even the borders of the online world have been creeping inward, with a new spate of smartphone bans and internet restrictions.

Marking the grim anniversary, a dozen women and girls have, at great risk to their safety, documented their lives for the world to see

Herat province
Every day, I wake up to the silence of dawn. I feel as though I am still holding my weapon. I lie on my bed for a few moments, taking deep breaths. With every awakening, I make a promise to myself: if my husband manages to return home safely today, I will thank God even more.
